summary: Convincing pay-and-display front fascia with legible tariff, keypad and ticket cup, but the rest of the cabinet is a plain dark box with blotchy wear.
critique: Proportions are right for a Flowbird Strada class unit. The H:W ratio reads about 3.1-3.5 against the reference 1674 x 475 x 379, and there is a plinth and a sloped rain hood. The front is the strongest part: a P & DISPLAY header, tariff card with prices, a small LCD showing £0.00, keypad, coin and card slots, contactless pad, green and red buttons, a TAKE TICKET cup that sticks out, and NO CHANGE GIVEN and PAY BY PHONE stickers. Most of it is texture on a flat plane, though. The fascia bezel is the only real depth, and at the close view the keypad, slots and display all look painted on. The hood is a thick flat slab with a hard square overhang. Real hoods are thin folded sheet with a drip edge and a slight radius. The back and both sides are one undifferentiated navy panel, apart from a ZEKO logo, an asset sticker and one lock. A real machine has a full-height service door with a visible shut-line, hinge side, a recessed cylinder lock, a vent grille, and often a solar panel on the hood. The wear is brown-orange cloudy blotches spread evenly over the lower body. It reads as dirty texture, not chipped powder coat. Real wear is edge chips to bare grey or galvanised metal on corners and the plinth, rain streaks from the hood seams, and sticker residue. The navy albedo is so dark that the sides go almost black in shade, which hides what form there is.
suggestions: Model the service door: a 2-3 mm inset shut-line groove round the front fascia and a second full-height door on the back, a hinge strip on one side, and a recessed round lock barrel (12-segment cylinder). Cost is about 150-250 tris.

Give the controls real relief. Recess the coin slot, card slot and display 5-8 mm. Push the keypad buttons out 2 mm, or use a normal map, and add a 1-2 mm lip round the display window with a glossy screen material (roughness 0.1) separate from the matte fascia.

Rebuild the hood as thin sheet: about 3 mm thick with a turned-down front drip lip and a 2-4 mm bevel. Optionally inset a dark solar-panel quad with a cell-grid texture on the top face. This costs fewer tris than the slab.

Replace the cloudy brown blotches with an edge-driven wear mask: chips to mid-grey metal (albedo ~0.45, roughness 0.5) on vertical corners, plinth edges and around the ticket cup, plus vertical grime streaks below the hood seam and the bezel corners. Keep the field paint clean.
Lift the navy albedo to roughly sRGB (35,55,110) and use a semi-gloss roughness of 0.35-0.45 so the sides pick up sky specular and stop reading as black.
Add side and back detail: a louvred vent panel near the top of one side, a council or operator info plate, and 4 visible anchor bolt heads at the plinth corners.
renderer_notes: The very dark side faces partly come from having no GI or bounce light in the viewer. A brighter albedo would still help.

summary: Clean, plausible louvred bollard light with a base flange, bolts and an access hatch, but it looks generic, the cap is faceted and the wear is dusty speckle.
critique: The silhouette is right for a common louvred bollard luminaire: a domed cap, an opal diffuser behind horizontal louvre rings with vertical support straps, a cylindrical body, and a flared base flange with nuts. The proportions look about 0.9-1.0 m tall by 0.2 m across. That is fine for a bollard light, though larger than the 450-600 x 100-110 reference. Problems: the cap and louvre rings show visible polygon facets in the silhouette, so they need more segments or smooth normals. The cap is too thick and puffy, like a mushroom. Real caps are thin spun aluminium with a crisp edge. The diffuser is a flat matte cream with no translucency and no inner lamp shape. The louvre rings have the same thickness and spacing from top to bottom, with no visible fixings. The body wear is a brown speckled noise that thickens towards the base. That reads as dirt spray rather than realistic splash-back, and it has the same density all the way round. The access hatch is a faint rectangle that barely shows. There are no labels, no cable-entry hints, and no mark where the bollard meets the ground: no soil or concrete collar, so the flange sits on top of the grass.
suggestions: Raise the radial segment count on the cap and louvre rings to 24-32, or make sure the normals are smoothed. The cap outline is the most visible flaw, and fixing it costs about 200 tris.
Thin the cap to a 15-20 mm lip with a slight dome and a crisp 2 mm edge bevel. Give the anodised aluminium a semi-gloss roughness of about 0.3.

Make the diffuser read as opal polycarbonate: a slight emissive term of 0.05-0.1, or a lighter albedo near (235,232,220) with roughness 0.2, and a faint horizontal ribbed normal. A darker core cylinder behind it would suggest the LED module.
Cut the access hatch as a real 1 mm groove with 2 tamper screws (small dark discs), and add a small manufacturer or IP-rating label sticker near the top of the body.

Swap the uniform brown speckle for a soil splash band only in the bottom 80-120 mm, darker and denser at the flange. Add a few scuffs at kick height. Leave the upper body clean, with slight dust on the top surfaces only.
Add a 300 mm square or round concrete footing decal or plate, flush with the ground, under the flange so it does not look placed on the lawn. This is a single quad plus a texture.

summary: Recognisable yellow slalom pole with a spring base, but the whole ground spike sits above the turf, and the pole itself is an untextured cylinder.
critique: The pole stands on the tip of its ground spike. The black spike and the spring coupling both hover above the grass, so the asset looks like it is balanced on a pin. On a real spring-base slalom pole, the 150-250 mm spike is pushed fully into the ground and the spring sits at or just above turf level. This is a placement and origin bug, and it is the single biggest realism break. The pole looks about 1.7 m long and roughly 25 mm across, which is plausible against the 1.0-1.5 m H, 25-32 mm reference, if a little tall. The yellow is a flat, slightly saturated matte with no sign of polypropylene sheen, no seam, and no scuffs or grass stains at the base. The top cap is a plain black cylinder. The spring is the only detail and is fine at distance.
suggestions: Move the pivot so the ground plane cuts the spike at the spring's lower collar. Bury the spike 150-200 mm, or simply omit its geometry below ground. Only the spring and the collar should sit above the turf.

Give the PVC/PP tube a slight gloss (roughness 0.35-0.45) and a saturated but not neon yellow, around sRGB (235,200,20). Add a faint vertical extrusion seam and scuff/grass-stain darkening in the bottom 200 mm via a vertical gradient mask. This needs no extra texture.
Model the top cap as a rounded rubber dome, a 3-ring hemisphere, about 8 mm proud of the tube, with a 1-2 mm lip.
Optional cheap variety: a second colour (red, blue, orange) via an instance tint parameter, and a 2-3 degree random lean per instance so rows of poles do not look laser-straight.
Keep the tris under 300; a 12-segment tube is enough.

summary: Correct rail-seat idea (post, top rail, flip-up shell), with a nicely ribbed seat underside, but the steelwork is blocky and bare and the shell looks thin and toy-like.
critique: The layout matches a safe-standing rail seat. There is a box-section post with a horizontal rail on top and a flip-up red shell on a hinge bar, shown in the locked-up position. The underside of the shell has believable moulded ribs and 2 fixing holes, and the hinge bracket with end bosses is a good touch. Weaknesses: the post is a sharp-edged square black bar with no bevels, no base plate, and no visible fixing. The 'bolts' are tiny floating dots on the grass instead of a welded base plate with 4 anchor bolts, or a side-fix to a terrace riser. The top rail is a plain round tube with a simple clamp. Real rails usually run continuously between posts, and when cut to one bay they need end caps. They often carry a seat or row number plate and are powder-coated or galvanised, with visible weld beads where post meets rail. The red shell is too thin at the edge, and its saturated, uniform toy-plastic red has no UV fade, no moulded seat number, and no mould texture. In the side view the shell and its curvature look like a curled sheet, and the bracket arms are simple blocks. Everything is clean, with no scuffs on the seat edge or the post base.
suggestions: Add a 150 x 150 x 10 mm base plate with 4 hex bolt heads, or a side-fix plate if it mounts to the riser, and bevel every post edge by 2-3 mm. That costs about 100 tris and fixes the 'floating dots'.
Fit end caps to the top rail (a domed plastic plug) and a small weld bead ring at the rail-to-post clamp. Add an aluminium row or seat number plate (60 x 30 mm decal) to the rail or post.

Thicken the shell rim to 4-5 mm with a rolled edge. Push the seat red slightly toward UV-faded, around sRGB (200,30,35) with roughness 0.45. Add a moulded seat-number disc and a faint stipple or mould-texture normal.

Use galvanised grey (albedo ~0.55, roughness 0.5, mottled) or a semi-gloss powder-coat black (albedo 0.05, roughness 0.35) for the steel instead of the current flat dark grey, with edge wear and some rust bloom at the base plate.
Refine the hinge bracket: rounded arms and a visible spindle with washers/nuts at each end. Keep it to about 200 tris, because these instance by the thousand.

summary: Recognisable free-kick mannequin silhouette, but it is a thin flat cut-out on a hovering spike, with crude anatomy and a splotchy mud mask.
critique: Real free-kick mannequins are blow-moulded hollow PE, about 1.8 m tall and 50-80 mm thick. They have soft, rounded edges, a clear head/neck/shoulder shape, often separate legs (or a central slot), moulded arms tight to the body, and a sturdy steel spike or weighted base. This one is a near-uniform slab about 20-30 mm thick with a flat front face. The edges have only a small round-over, so in the side view it reads as a plank. The head is a narrow pointed oval with no neck taper. The shoulders are a single curve, and there are no arms and no hip break. A shallow groove fakes the legs, and the leg bottoms are cut square. The embossed logo panel is a nice idea, but the glyph is unreadable. The mount repeats the agility-pole bug: the stub post, the spring and the spike all sit above the grass and the mannequin hovers about 0.3 m up. The post also barely enters the bottom edge of the board, so the connection looks weak and unexplained. The mud on the lower legs is a pitted noise of round craters with hard edges. It reads as acid damage, not mud splash. The yellow albedo is flat and slightly olive in shade.
suggestions: Fix the mount. Bury the spike so the spring sits at turf level and the leg bottoms are 50-100 mm above the grass. Run a visible steel socket tube 200-300 mm up the back of the legs with 2 bolts, so the board is clearly carried.

Give it body. Inflate the profile to 60-80 mm thick with a fully rounded edge (6-8 segment half-round) and a slightly convex front and back, like a blow-moulded part. Use about 1-1.5k tris for the whole figure.

Improve the anatomy in the outline: a neck narrower than the head, sloped shoulders, arms moulded to the body with a slight gap or groove, a waist taper and a real leg split (a 30-50 mm gap from the crotch to the feet), and rounded feet.

Replace the crater noise with a soft mud-splash gradient. Use dark brown (90,70,45) at about 60% opacity in the bottom 300 mm, fading upward with streaky drips, plus scuffs and boot-mark smudges at shin height. Use roughness 0.6 for the mud and 0.4 for the clean plastic.
Make the embossed panel a legible maker logo or number (a crisp normal-map decal) and add a small moulded-in hanging hole near the head, which real ones have for storage racks.

summary: Believable tall training cone with pole slots and a rolled base, but the plastic is flat and soft-looking and the slots are crude square holes.
critique: The shape is right for a multi-purpose training cone that takes poles and hurdle bars: a tall open-top frustum about 450 mm high, a wider rolled foot, and side holes. Problems: the holes are small square cutouts at odd, irregular positions. On real cones the slots are arranged in a regular pattern at 2-3 heights, sized for 25-32 mm poles, often rectangular with radiused corners, in opposite pairs so a pole passes straight through. Here they look randomly scattered. The base lip is a soft rounded bulge. Real cones have a crisp moulded ring, sometimes a flat skirt about 240 mm across, with a visible wall thickness at the open bottom. The top opening is a plain cut with little visible wall thickness. The surface carries faint scratch lines but otherwise reads as matte clay. Soft PE cones have a light semi-gloss sheen, a moulded maker logo, size text, and scuffs or grass and mud near the foot. The orange is good. The wall looks too thick at the slots, which shows as chunky orange reveals.
suggestions: Lay out the slots as 3 levels x 2 opposed pairs (or 4 around), each 35 x 15 mm with 3 mm corner radii, and align each pair so a pole axis passes through. Keep the wall 2-3 mm so the reveals are thin.
Define the foot: a 240 mm base with a crisp 6-8 mm rim and a small step up to the cone wall, and a visible thin open edge where the cone meets the ground. Cost is about 100 tris.
Use semi-gloss PE: roughness 0.35-0.4 with a slight subsurface-ish lift (raise the albedo a touch in grazing light), plus a moulded logo or '45 cm' emboss as a normal-map decal.
Add a wear mask: grass/mud darkening on the bottom 40 mm, and a few scuffs and creases on the upper half from being stacked. These show in the close view and cost only texture.
renderer_notes: The grass blades around the foot have no contact darkening, which comes from the lack of ambient occlusion in the viewer, not from the asset.

summary: A leafy, well-shaded canopy, but it reads as an umbrella acacia or small ornamental tree, not a mature English oak: the trunk is far too short and thin and the crown is flat and lopsided.
critique: An English oak (Quercus robur) has a massive buttressed trunk 0.8-1.5 m across, a clear bole of 3-6 m, then a few huge twisting limbs. It has a broad, rounded, slightly irregular dome crown, roughly as wide as or wider than it is tall, and lobed leaves that give a fine, clumpy texture. This asset has a slim trunk that splits into thin straight radiating branches very low, at about a fifth of the height. The crown is a flattened umbrella, wider than tall, pushed heavily to one side. It overhangs the trunk to the left in one view and to the right in another. That gives a parasol-pine, acacia or windswept-hawthorn silhouette. The trunk-to-crown ratio is about 1:25, where an oak would be about 1:12-1:15. The branches are smooth tubes of constant radius with no taper or kinks and no bark texture visible at this distance. The leaf cards are large and read as oversized paper clumps at the closer view, with no oak-leaf lobing. The top view is the best angle: varied clumps, good self-shadowing and good colour variation. The shadow shows nice dappled gaps.
suggestions: Fix the structure first. Use a clear bole of 3-5 m and a trunk of 1.0-1.2 m at breast height with root flare at the base (a 4-6 lobe buttress, about 30% wider at ground). Then 3-5 primary limbs that leave the trunk at 40-70 degrees and kink as they go, not thin straight spokes.

Reshape the crown to a broad dome. Aim for a height of 18-22 m to a spread of 18-22 m, centred over the trunk with only mild asymmetry (offset under 15% of spread). Fill the upper middle so it is not flat-topped.

Taper the branches (radius falling about 0.7x per fork) with gnarled bends, and give the trunk a deep-fissured bark texture with a strong normal map (vertical plates and cracks), albedo around (70,60,50).

Shrink the leaf cards by about 40-50%, increase the count to compensate, and use an oak-leaf alpha atlas (lobed outlines) with some cards back-facing in darker, yellower green. Budget about 8-15k tris for LOD0 and an impostor card for distance, which keeps it instanceable for perimeter planting.
Add 2-3 dead twigs/snags poking out of the crown silhouette and a few gaps showing sky through the crown. Those breaks in the outline are what make oaks read at distance.
renderer_notes: The flat lawn and distant field textures are environment, not the asset. Foliage lighting is reasonable for a forward renderer without GI.
